title: Application Allowlisting
summary: Application allowlisting, also called application control, is an endpoint control that permits only approved executables, scripts and libraries to run and blocks everything else by default. Enforcement happens in the kernel before a process is created, and each rule identifies a program by publisher signature, cryptographic hash, or path, usually with a fallback mode that records blocked attempts before it starts blocking them. Because the model is inverted relative to deny listing, it defeats novel droppers, ransomware binaries and unsigned tooling that signature based antivirus has never seen, and it frustrates an intruder whose next step needs an unapproved tool. The operational cost is real: patched binaries break hash rules, line of business and engineering tools need a governed approval path, and scripts run from temporary folders create constant exceptions. The mistake organisations make is leaving the policy in audit only mode for years, which records violations while preventing nothing and quietly turns a strong control into shelfware.

beginner.definition: Application allowlisting is a control that only lets approved programs run on a computer. Everything else is blocked by default. The computer checks each program before that program starts. This is the opposite of a blocklist, which names the programs that are forbidden.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers usually need to run their own program on your computer. If only approved programs may run, their program simply cannot start. This stops new malware that no scanner has seen before. The cost is effort, because every new tool must be approved first. Without a good approval process, users get blocked and work stops.
howItWorks: The team builds a list of programs that are allowed to run.
Each entry may use a publisher signature, a file hash or a path.
A small agent on the computer checks every program against that approved list.
Approved programs start normally, so users often notice nothing at all in daily work.
Blocked programs do not start, and the attempt is written to a log.
Administrators review those logs and add new tools through a proper process.
beginner.example: Think of a members only club with a doorman. He holds a list of names and lets only those people in. A stranger with a very good story still waits outside. If a member changes their name and forgets to tell the doorman, they wait outside too. Allowlisting has the same strength and the same kind of annoyance.
takeaways: Allowlisting blocks unknown programs, including malware nobody has seen yet.
Plan the approval process first, or blocked users will demand it be switched off.
Use publisher signatures where possible, because patches break hash based rules.

objectives: Explain how allowlisting differs from blocklisting and antivirus signatures.
Describe how a program's identity can be established by signature, hash or path.
Explain why audit mode is a temporary step and not a finished deployment.
Describe the approval and exception process a working allowlist policy requires.
Identify the log sources that show blocked execution attempts on endpoints.
